Chapter 4: Rethinking Procreation as a Moral Issue
For most of us, having kids just feels like a natural part of life. You know, it’s often seen as a personal decision—a source of so much joy and meaning. Society encourages us to have children, celebrates every new birth, and almost never questions whether bringing someone new into the world is actually the right thing to do.
But what if we really stop and think about the harm that can come with simply existing? Suddenly, the whole idea of procreation starts to look a lot more complicated.
Picture a couple sitting together, talking about whether to start a family. They share their hopes, their dreams, even their worries. Of course, they want their child to have a good life—to pass on their love and their values. But as their conversation deepens, something changes. They start to realize this decision isn’t just about them. It’s about the person they’d bring into existence, and all the pain and challenges that person is bound to face.
Most people treat procreation as something private, like it only affects the parents. But in reality, it’s a choice with huge consequences for the new person who’s created. That child will go through pain, loss, and—eventually—death. There’ll be struggles and difficulties, some totally unpredictable and impossible to avoid.
The couple starts to understand: they can’t guarantee their child’s happiness. Sure, they can offer a loving home, but they can’t shield them from every hurt. The world is full of risks, and suffering—well, it’s something every single life has to face. By choosing to have a child, they’re also choosing to expose someone to all that risk.
That realization is unsettling, isn’t it? It really challenges the idea that procreation is always positive. Suddenly, bringing someone into existence isn’t just about hope and love—it’s about harm and risk, too. The couple begins to see that deciding to have a child is, at its core, a moral question—not just a personal one.
Society doesn’t often talk about this side of things. We celebrate births, and when people decide not to have children, they’re often met with confusion or even pity. But once we recognize the harm that can come simply from being born, procreation becomes a real ethical question. It’s not enough to just hope for the best, or to assume life is always worth living. We have to face the risks and potential harms honestly.
So now, the couple sits quietly, really thinking about what they’ve learned. They realize that having a child isn’t just about fulfilling their own dreams—it’s about taking on responsibility for the suffering their child will undoubtedly face.
And that changes everything about how they see the world, and the choices they make.
